freeResponseAndWritingGuidance.question: Sketch 1 and 3/2 on equal bars and on a number line. Name the whole and explain why 3/2 exceeds 1.
freeResponseAndWritingGuidance.acceptableReasoning: One bar is one kilogram and each interval of length one is one kilogram. Mark 1 at 4/4, and 3/2 at six quarters, or one and a half equal bars. Two extra quarters beyond one explain why 3/2 > 1.
freeResponseAndWritingGuidance.feedback: Use the example reasoning to locate the unsupported step; accept different wording with valid evidence. This is formative feedback, not an official mark.

freeResponseAndWritingGuidance.question: Draw 6/4 on equal area bars, mark it on a number line and name the whole. Explain why it is beyond one.
freeResponseAndWritingGuidance.acceptableReasoning: Shade a full four-quarter bar and two quarters of an equal bar. Mark six quarter-steps from zero at 1.5. The amount is 6/4 of the named whole, so it exceeds 1.
freeResponseAndWritingGuidance.feedback: Use the example reasoning to locate the unsupported step; accept different wording with valid evidence. This is formative feedback, not an official mark.

freeResponseAndWritingGuidance.question: Order 3/4, 1/2 and 5/8. Use benchmarks and a number line to justify.
freeResponseAndWritingGuidance.acceptableReasoning: 1/2 < 5/8 < 3/4 because they are 4/8, 5/8 and 6/8. All lie between the one-half and one benchmarks. A number line shows this order left to right.

freeResponseAndWritingGuidance.question: Find 3/4 + 1/8 exactly. Also draw 6/4 on equal area bars and explain what one whole means.
freeResponseAndWritingGuidance.acceptableReasoning: 3/4 + 1/8 = 6/8 + 1/8 = 7/8. Accept 14/16 and exact decimal 0.875. For 6/4 show one full bar and two quarter-pieces of an equal bar. The whole must be fixed and named.

freeResponseAndWritingGuidance.acceptableReasoning: 3/4 - 1/3 = 9/12 - 4/12 = 5/12 kg. Accept any exactly equivalent fraction. The explicit two-place estimate is approximately 0.42 kg. It is positive because 9 > 4 and below 3/4 because a positive amount was removed. Do not equate 0.42 with 5/12.

scenes.title: Explain latent heat and evaporation
scenes.learnerAction: Use the model, complete its task, and explain what the representation shows.

content.body:
Latent heat is energy absorbed or released during a change of state without a temperature change in this ideal model. It changes the arrangement and separation associated with attractions between particles, rather than increasing average kinetic energy. Melting and vaporization absorb energy; freezing and condensation release it. These reversible physical changes preserve water molecules.

Evaporation happens at a liquid surface even below boiling temperature. Some surface molecules escape into the gas. Boiling forms vapor bubbles throughout the liquid at its boiling temperature for the pressure. Invisible water vapor is gas; visible mist contains tiny liquid droplets.

How a seed library works. A seed library is a shared collection of seeds for planting. In this invented school example, families contribute in several ways. Some donate seeds; others clean storage tins or teach pupils when to plant. No family must pay money to take part. Pupils label each tin with the seed type and record each loan. The record helps the group know what is available. Borrowers return some seeds after their harvest so the collection can be used again. As a result, more pupils can borrow seeds in the next planting season. Dry storage helps protect the collection. Damp seeds may develop mould and become unsuitable for planting. Pupils inspect the tins each week and keep them in a dry cupboard. This example explains a possible system; it does not report measured results from a real school.
